title: Parallel LCR Circuit
short_intro: A parallel LCR circuit is an alternating current network where an inductor, a capacitor, and a resistor are connected in parallel across a sinusoidal voltage source. It functions as a rejector circuit because its impedance is maximum and the current is minimum at resonance.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Conditions for parallel resonance, resonance frequency formula, phase relationship between voltage and branch currents, and basic numericals on impedance and current at resonance.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Admittance and susceptance analysis, dynamic resistance at resonance, quality factor derivation, sharpness of resonance, and bandwidth in parallel resonant circuits.

prerequisites: Concept of admittance, conductance, and susceptance in AC circuits

concept_notes.heading: Circuit Configuration and Phasor Relations
bullets: In a parallel LCR circuit, a pure resistor of resistance R, a pure inductor of inductance L, and an ideal capacitor of capacitance C are connected in parallel across an AC source of voltage V = V<sub>0</sub>sin(ωt).
The alternating voltage across each parallel branch is the same, whereas the branch currents (I<sub>R</sub>, I<sub>L</sub>, I<sub>C</sub>) differ in phase relative to the common voltage.

The current through the resistor (I<sub>R</sub>) is in phase with the voltage, the current through the inductor (I<sub>L</sub>) lags the voltage by 90°, and the current through the capacitor (I<sub>C</sub>) leads the voltage by 90°.

concept_notes.heading: Parallel Resonance Phenomenon
bullets: Parallel resonance occurs when the reactive component of the total current is zero, meaning the inductive susceptance equals the capacitive susceptance.
At resonance, the reactive branch currents (I<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>C</sub>) are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase, completely canceling each other out in the external circuit.
Consequently, the total line current drawn from the source is solely determined by the resistive branch and is at its minimum value, making the circuit impedance maximum.

concept_notes.heading: Dynamic Resistance at Resonance
bullets: At resonance, the parallel LCR circuit acts as a pure resistance known as the dynamic resistance or rejector resistance.
The expression for dynamic resistance is given by R<sub>d</sub> = L / (CR), which can also be written as Z<sub>max</sub> = L / (CR).
Since L, C, and R are typical laboratory values, the dynamic resistance can be very large, resulting in a very small total current at resonance.

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor (Q-factor) and Bandwidth
bullets: The quality factor Q of a parallel LCR circuit is defined as the ratio of the circulating reactive current in the LC tank to the total supply current at resonance.
It is also expressed as Q = ω<sub>r</sub>CR = R / (ω<sub>r</sub>L), which is the inverse of the series LCR circuit Q-factor expression.
The bandwidth (BW) of the resonance curve is given by BW = f<sub>r</sub> / Q = 1 / (2πRC), determining the selectivity of the circuit.

derivations.title: Resonance Frequency and Impedance of Parallel LCR Circuit
derivations.conditions: Ideal parallel LCR circuit connected to an AC source of angular frequency ω
steps: Write the admittance Y of the parallel combination: Y = G + j(B<sub>C</sub> - B<sub>L</sub>), where conductance G = 1/R, capacitive susceptance B<sub>C</sub> = ωC, and inductive susceptance B<sub>L</sub> = 1/(ωL).
Substitute the terms into the admittance equation: Y = (1/R) + j(ωC - 1/(ωL)).
The total impedance Z is the reciprocal of admittance: Z = 1 / sqrt((1/R²) + (ωC - 1/(ωL))²).
At resonance, the imaginary part of admittance becomes zero: ω<sub>r</sub>C - 1/(ω<sub>r</sub>L) = 0.
Solve for the resonant angular frequency: ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / sqrt(LC).
derivations.result: Resonant frequency f_r = (1 / 2π) * sqrt(1 / LC) and maximum impedance Z_max = L / (CR)

derivations.title: Derivation of Quality Factor (Q-factor)
steps: Define Q-factor as the ratio of magnitude of inductive (or capacitive) current to the total supply current at resonance: Q = I<sub>C</sub> / I<sub>R</sub>.
Express the currents in terms of voltage V: I<sub>C</sub> = V(ω<sub>r</sub>C) and I<sub>R</sub> = V / R.
Substitute the currents into the Q-factor ratio: Q = V(ω<sub>r</sub>C) / (V / R) = ω<sub>r</sub>CR.
Substitute ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / sqrt(LC) into the equation: Q = (1 / sqrt(LC)) * CR = R * sqrt(C / L).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frequency Response: Impedance vs Frequency
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve plotting Impedance (Z) on the y-axis against Frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing a sharp peak at f = f_r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Impedance reaches its maximum value (Z_max = L/CR) at the resonant frequency f_r, causing the circuit to reject currents of this frequency.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual MCQs on why parallel LCR circuits are called rejector circuits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frequency Response: Current vs Frequency
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A dip-shaped curve plotting Line Current (I) on the y-axis against Frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing a sharp minimum at f = f_r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Line current drops to a minimum value (I = V/Z_max) at resonance because inductive and capacitive susceptances cancel each other out.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate understanding of minimum current conditions in rejector circuits.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Angle vs Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sigmoid-like curve plotting phase angle (φ) on the y-axis against frequency (f) on the x-axis, crossing zero at f_r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Below resonance (ω < ω<sub>r</sub>), the circuit is inductive (φ < 0); at resonance, φ = 0; above resonance (ω > ω<sub>r</sub>), the circuit is capacitive (φ > 0).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in PGT questions regarding the inductive and capacitive behavior of the circuit off-resonance.

solved_numericals.question: A parallel LCR circuit has an inductor of 0.2 H, a capacitor of 5 μF, and a resistor of 100 Ω connected across a 220 V AC source. Calculate the resonant frequency of the circuit.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 0.2 H, C = 5 × 10<sup>-6</sup> F, R = 100 Ω.
Recall the resonance frequency formula: f_r = (1 / 2π) * sqrt(1 / LC).
Calculate square root of LC: sqrt(LC) = sqrt(1 × 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 1 × 10<sup>-3</sup> s.
Substitute into the frequency formula: f_r = 1 / (2 × 3.1416 × 1 × 10<sup>-3</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: Find the dynamic resistance and the minimum current at resonance for a parallel LCR circuit with L = 2 H, C = 0.5 μF, and R = 50 Ω, when driven by a 100 V AC source.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 2 H, C = 0.5 × 10<sup>-6</sup> F, R = 50 Ω, V = 100 V.
Recall the formula for dynamic resistance: Z<sub>max</sub> = L / (CR).
Calculate minimum line current at resonance: I<sub>min</sub> = V / Z<sub>max</sub> = 100 / 80000 = 1.25 × 10<sup>-3</sup> A.
solved_numericals.answer: Dynamic resistance = 80 kΩ, Minimum current = 1.25 mA

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the quality factor and bandwidth of a parallel LCR circuit having L = 1 H, C = 1 μF, and R = 1000 Ω at resonance.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 1 H, C = 1 × 10<sup>-6</sup> F, R = 1000 Ω.
Calculate resonant frequency f<sub>r</sub>: f<sub>r</sub> = 1 / (2π sqrt(LC)) = 1 / (2 × 3.1416 × sqrt(1 × 1 × 10<sup>-6</sup>)) = 159.15 Hz.
Calculate Q-factor using Q = R * sqrt(C / L): Q = 1000 * sqrt(1 × 10<sup>-6</sup> / 1) = 1000 × 10<sup>-3</sup> = 1.

assumptions_and_limitations: The inductor is assumed to have negligible resistance, or its resistance is lumped into the total branch resistance R.
The source is assumed to be an ideal sinusoidal voltage source with zero internal resistance.
The formulas for parallel resonance assume high Q-factor approximations (ω<sub>r</sub> ≈ 1 / sqrt(LC)) where exact resonance and anti-resonance frequencies converge.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Parallel LCR circuits have maximum current at resonance.
common_misconceptions.correct: Parallel LCR circuits have minimum current at resonance.
common_misconceptions.why: At resonance, the impedance is maximum (dynamic resistance), which minimizes the total line current drawn from the source.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The resonance frequency formula for parallel LCR is different from series LCR.
common_misconceptions.correct: The ideal resonance frequency formula f_r = 1 / (2πsqrt(LC)) is identical for both ideal series and parallel LCR circuits.
common_misconceptions.why: Both circuits achieve resonance when the net reactive susceptance or reactance becomes zero, yielding the same unconditioned angular frequency expression.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Branch currents are zero at parallel resonance.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the net external line current is minimum; individual branch currents (I<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>C</sub>) can be very large.
common_misconceptions.why: A large circulating current flows between the inductor and capacitor inside the parallel tank circuit due to energy oscillation.

quick_revision: A parallel LCR circuit acts as a rejector circuit because its impedance is maximum at resonance.
At parallel resonance, total line current is minimum and in phase with the applied voltage (φ = 0).
Dynamic resistance of a parallel LCR circuit is given by Z<sub>max</sub> = L / (CR).
The quality factor Q for a parallel LCR circuit is expressed as Q = ω<sub>r</sub>CR = R * sqrt(C / L).
